newsitem.title: FRANCE: FIS says Algeria poll will resolve nothing.
newsitem.headline: FIS says Algeria poll will resolve nothing.

text.p: Algeria's outlawed Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) said on Wednesday that parliamentary elections in Algeria next week would not solve the country's crisis, and urged talks to end five years of bloodshed.

"The legislative elections under way will resolve nothing without the participation of all political parties including the Islamic Salvation Front," it said in a statement faxed from Germany to an international news agency in Paris.
"The reintegration of the FIS in the political field is a political necessity if one is searching sincerely to rebuild a country reconciled with itself."
Algeria on June 5 holds its first parliamentary election since the authorities in January 1992 cancelled the last such poll after the fundamentalist FIS had taken a massive lead.
Violence erupted shortly afterwards and about 60,000 people have since been killed.
The FIS, which says it reflects the voice of Algeria's 29 million people, is an outlawed body and cannot take part in the elections.
Many earlier FIS statements had demanded freedom for its jailed leaders Abassi Madani and Ali Belhadj as a condition for dialogue. The latest statement made no mention of this.
Entitled "For a strategy to get out of the crisis in Algeria", the statement said the FIS did not believe either side could achieve military victory, despite the odds favouring the authorities.
"The political way out seems to us to be at the same time the only and best solution to the conflict. It demands from the two protagonists a mutual recognition and concessions by both."
The FIS called for face-to-face talks with the authorities followed by multilateral talks.

"A national conference should work to create the necessary conditions for a return to stability in the country and consolidation of the republic's institutions, guaranteeing the right of each and everyone," it said.

It recalled that it had condemned "all attacks and all actions which affect innocent people" and said it held itself resolutely on the side ot its people to fight all those who attacked their "honour, dignity and sovereignty".
Officials blamed the FIS and its armed wing, the Islamic Salvation Army, for much of the early violence, mainly between Islamists and security forces.
Much of this has been eclipsed by the killing of civilians by bombs and night massacres in villages in which none has been spared, including young children.

Many of these killings have been blamed on the Armed Islamic Group (GIA). In the worst mass killing, 93 people in one village died earlier this year. Most choked to death after their throats were cut.
